articles.title: Over the last several weeks, something has been changing.
articles.subtitle: I did not expect this many people to understand.
articles.author: David Sicairos
articles.html:
Over the last several weeks, something has been changing.

I did not expect this many people to understand.

The messages are changing.

The conversations are changing.

And the people reaching out are changing.

At first, much of this work felt like a personal effort to understand what happened to me, what the public record could show, and what people are supposed to do when a system feels unclear or unfair.

That part is still real.

But the work is no longer only about one story.

I am hearing from people who have spent years inside education.

People who understand what it means to care about students while also seeing the pressure, the politics, the silence, and the decisions that can leave families and employees feeling unheard.

I am hearing from people who do not just want to complain about the system.

They want to help change it.

That matters.

Support from someone who knows education

One of the messages that stayed with me this week came from Alberto Velarde.

Alberto is a 34-year education veteran who also ran for Merced County Superintendent of Schools.

He understands the work from inside education, and he understands why communities need leaders who are willing to study the evidence, ask clear questions, and focus on what students, families, and employees actually need.

In his message, he wrote about the courage it takes to pursue doctoral research and use evidence to examine systems that may be failing students, treating employees unfairly, or losing the community’s trust.

We need leaders who understand the system and are willing to do the work to make it better.

That kind of support means a lot to me.

Not because I need anyone to agree with every conclusion I may reach.

But because it reminds me that experienced educators understand the difference between noise and serious work.

They understand that research matters.

Evidence matters.

Documentation matters.

And real leadership is not about protecting a title.

It is about serving people honestly when the work gets difficult.

[INSERT ALBERTO VELARDE SCREENSHOT HERE]

Alberto Velarde, a 34-year education veteran and former candidate for Merced County Superintendent of Schools, on research, evidence, and leadership that serves people.

Building with people who want change

This is bigger than one person.

More people are reaching out who understand that education needs more than polished language, symbolic appreciation, or closed-door decision-making.

They know students deserve real support.

They know teachers deserve more than symbolic appreciation.

They know families deserve more than being told to trust a process they cannot see or understand.

And they know that public service should mean something.

As this work develops, I am grateful to be building relationships with people who want to do the work alongside one another: people who care about students, fairness, clear information, and better leadership.

What I am learning from the support

I am learning that the people who get it are not looking for a hero.

They are looking for doers.

People willing to read before reacting.

People willing to ask a clear question.

People willing to look at a budget, policy, board agenda, public record, or timeline and say:

Help me understand what this means.

That is the culture I want to help build through 209 Media Connect and 209 Audit.

Not a culture built on outrage.

Not a culture built on personal attacks.

A culture built on information, responsibility, courage, and a shared belief that students, families, educators, and communities deserve better.

What is moving forward

The public-information work is continuing.

I received new materials last week and am reviewing them carefully.

I am continuing my doctoral studies in Organizational Leadership, where I am learning more about systems, leadership culture, student support, and the ways institutions can either create trust or create barriers.

I am also continuing to build 209 Media Connect into a place where public questions, personal updates, leadership lessons, and community learning can live together.

The work is becoming clearer.

Not because every question has been answered.

But because more people are helping identify which questions matter.

The person doing the work matters too

I also want to be honest about something else.

This kind of work requires structure.

It requires enough rest to think clearly.

Enough discipline to keep studying.

Enough routine to keep moving when the work feels heavy.

That is why dBeastco Wellness is part of this story too.

The Intentional Morning Blueprint is not about pretending every day will be easy.

It is about giving yourself a more grounded way to begin.

A few minutes to reset.

A way to decide what matters.

A reminder that you can care about big systems and still take care of the person doing the work.

If you want the first version of the Intentional Morning Blueprint, reply or DM:

MORNING

A question for you

What does better leadership look like to you?

Not the title.

Not the campaign language.

Not the public statement.

The actual behavior.

Reply with one thing you believe good leaders should do when students, families, educators, or employees raise a difficult question.

I read the replies.

David Sicairos
